name: Delayed puberty
aliases: constitutional delay of growth and puberty

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Delayed puberty is defined as the absence of secondary sexual characteristics by an age about two to two-and-a-half standard deviations beyond the population mean, conventionally around age thirteen in girls and fourteen in boys
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the commonest cause, is more frequent in boys, often runs in families, and represents a normal variant rather than disease
The key diagnostic distinction is between hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (low gonadotrophins, a central problem) and hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism (high gonadotrophins, primary gonadal failure)
Elevated gonadotrophins point to primary gonadal failure such as Turner syndrome in girls or Klinefelter syndrome in boys
Low gonadotrophins may reflect constitutional delay, chronic illness, undernutrition, excessive exercise, or permanent causes such as Kallmann syndrome and pituitary disease
Bone age assessment helps, since it is delayed but consistent with pubertal potential in constitutional delay
Distinguishing constitutional delay from isolated gonadotrophin deficiency can be difficult and may require a period of observation or specialist testing
Management ranges from reassurance and monitoring in constitutional delay to treating the underlying disorder and, where appropriate, carefully induced pubertal hormone therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Puberty begins with reactivation of pulsatile hypothalamic gonadotrophin-releasing hormone secretion, which stimulates pituitary LH and FSH and thereby gonadal steroid production and gametogenesis. Delayed puberty results from any interruption of this axis. In constitutional delay the axis is intrinsically normal but activates late, with a correspondingly delayed bone age. Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism arises from functional suppression (chronic disease, malnutrition, intense athletic training, eating disorders, hyperprolactinaemia) or permanent central defects (Kallmann syndrome with anosmia, other congenital GnRH deficiencies, pituitary tumours or infiltration). Hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism reflects primary gonadal failure, as in chromosomal disorders (Turner, Klinefelter), gonadal dysgenesis, or damage from chemotherapy or radiation, where absent negative feedback drives gonadotrophins high.
additionalDifferentials: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Functional hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism from chronic illness, undernutrition, or excessive exercise
Kallmann syndrome and other congenital GnRH deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Basal LH, FSH, and sex steroid measurement to separate central from primary gonadal causes
Bone age radiograph to assess skeletal maturation and pubertal potential
Karyotype when a chromosomal disorder is suspected
Prolactin, thyroid function, and screening for chronic systemic disease
Pituitary and hypothalamic imaging when a central structural cause is considered
redFlags: Anosmia with absent puberty suggesting Kallmann syndrome
Neurological features such as headache or visual disturbance indicating a hypothalamic-pituitary tumour
Short stature with characteristic features raising suspicion of Turner syndrome
Evidence of a chronic systemic illness or eating disorder underlying the delay
reference.prognosis: Constitutional delay carries an excellent prognosis with spontaneous progression through normal puberty and attainment of adult height and fertility; outcomes in pathological causes depend on the specific disorder and on timely diagnosis and hormone replacement.
pitfalls: Labelling all delay as constitutional and missing a treatable or serious underlying cause
Overlooking anosmia, which would point to Kallmann syndrome
Failing to consider chronic illness, undernutrition, or an eating disorder as functional causes
Not arranging a karyotype in suspected Turner or Klinefelter syndrome
management: Reassurance and watchful waiting in constitutional delay of growth and puberty, a normal variant, with monitoring of pubertal progression and growth velocity
Short-course low-dose sex-steroid priming (testosterone in boys, oestrogen in girls) to induce puberty and accelerate growth where delay causes psychosocial distress
Long-term sex-hormone replacement for permanent hypogonadism to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, titrated to mimic normal pubertal progression

Treat underlying causes: optimise nutrition, manage chronic illness, address excessive exercise or eating disorders in functional hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, and treat hyperprolactinaemia or pituitary disease
Fertility-directed therapy where relevant, using pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone or gonadotrophins in hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism when fertility is desired
Monitor growth, bone age and bone health with bone-protective measures given hypogonadism-related low bone density
Multidisciplinary paediatric endocrinology and psychology input, with karyotype and genetic counselling for chromosomal causes such as Turner and Klinefelter syndromes and for Kallmann syndrome
